title: Flood and water restoration
estimatedMinutesNote: Estimated, not verified. Rule: learner text 3317 words / 100 per minute + 3 min per knowledge check (12) + 5 min allowance, rounded to nearest 5, minimum 15.

instruction.heading: Module authority and restricted work
instruction.body: This module is training content. It does not grant authority to enter a flood-affected building, to carry out regulated flood restoration, to energise or isolate electrical, gas or solar systems, to remove sewage or contaminated water, to dispose of waste, or to certify that a property is dry, hygienic, structurally sound or safe to occupy. Completing this lesson does not give a licence, certificate or approval. Some of the work described is restricted to licensed, authorised or specially trained people, including electrical and gas work, structural assessment, sewage handling and some disposal. The site controller, the owner, the insurer and the competent professionals each hold separate decisions, and none of them replaces the others. Where the controlling authority or the competent professional is not identified, stop and refer.

instruction.heading: 1. Site release, permissions and restoration scope
instruction.body: Site release, permissions and restoration scope need a documented decision based on the facts of the site, not on assumptions. Distinguish an observable condition from a qualified technical determination. A customer request, an insurer authorisation and a professional safety clearance are three separate documents, and none of them can be treated as the others. Start a scope sheet that names the party responsible for access, for utilities and for environmental hazards. Confirm the site authority and the approved procedure, identify who can make the technical decision, set the exclusions, and then collect only the information that can be gathered safely. Record each unresolved uncertainty. Stop work when permission, controls or competent supervision are missing. Produce an access decision that names the approver, the date, the zones, the limits on activity and the unresolved hazards. Never turn an observation into a technical certificate.

instruction.heading: 2. Floodwater origin and contamination screening
instruction.body: Water appearance cannot prove that the water is biologically safe. Consider the possible sources of contamination before selecting a work scope: sewage entry, outdoor floodwater, chemical release, the time since the intrusion and the risk of cross-contamination. Produce a contamination uncertainty log. Do not assign a contamination category on the basis of odour or colour. Treat unknown contamination as a stop-work concern and refer its classification to competent personnel. Pass the observations, the uncertainties and the next authorised decision to the receiving supervisor.

instruction.heading: 3. Structural instability, slips and confined spaces
instruction.body: Water can conceal weakened ceilings, unstable stored loads, undermined flooring and blocked escape routes. Floors that look sound may be slippery, and spaces under floors or behind walls may be confined. Visual inspection is not structural clearance. Exclude any area that has not been cleared, record the exclusion zones and evacuation paths, and request a qualified structural assessment. Submit the engineering referral records with the scope sheet. Do not enter a confined space or an undermined area to look for the problem.

instruction.heading: 4. Electrical, gas and solar system hazards
instruction.body: Water-exposed power outlets, damaged cables, gas appliances, and solar and battery systems can remain hazardous even when they appear to be switched off. A cleaner cannot certify that a system has been isolated. Create a utility verification checklist that names the authorised professional and the energisation that is prohibited. Do not energise any water-affected system until a licensed clearance has been issued. Do not attempt to isolate, reconnect or test electrical or gas equipment. Refer each hazard to the authorised professional and record the referral.

instruction.heading: 5. PPE, hygiene and biological exposure
instruction.body: Biological contamination can reach workers through broken skin, mucous membranes, inhalation or ingestion. Controls must follow the site hazard assessment, the training held by each worker and the washing facilities that are actually available. Record each exposure route, the hygiene limitations and the escalation route to a supervisor or to occupational-health advice. Suspend exposure work until suitable controls and hygiene facilities have been provided. Where an exposure occurs, follow the employer's incident and medical referral procedure, and keep the record confidential.

instruction.heading: 6. Moisture mapping and baseline records
instruction.body: Moisture readings depend on the instrument type, the material and the reference conditions, so a reading without its method cannot be compared with another. A single number cannot independently prove drying or safe occupancy. Record the material, the instrument, the locations and the baseline before work begins. Keep a measurement register that shows the instrument identifier, the method, the material, the location, the time and the limitations. Require calibrated and appropriate measurement, with expert interpretation of the results.

instruction.heading: 7. Water removal planning and equipment limitations
instruction.body: Water-removal equipment must be suitable for the contamination and the location. Its use depends on a safe electrical supply and on trained operators. Capacity alone is not a selection criterion, because a machine that is large enough but unsuitable for the contamination or the power supply creates new hazards. Before any work, create an equipment suitability and authorisation matrix. Confirm that the utilities are safe, that the operators are trained and that the equipment suits the contamination before the work starts.

instruction.heading: 8. Porous contents, salvage and contamination
instruction.body: Porous furnishings, insulation and wallboard may keep contamination that cannot be seen on the surface, so a visual wipe-down is not sufficient evidence of restoration. Quarantine the items and defer any decision to restore or dispose of them to an authorised, competent assessment. Prepare a chain-of-decision record that links the identity of each item, the contamination concern, the owner's consent and the authority for its disposition. Keep the record so that any later decision can be traced back to the evidence.

instruction.heading: 9. Drying principles and monitoring logs
instruction.body: Restoration progress is a measured trend, not simply a finish that looks dry. Covering a surface too early can trap moisture and hide damage. Prepare a monitoring chart and an escalation notice for any moisture that remains unresolved. Do not set universal pass thresholds in a training or operational document, because the appropriate values depend on the material, the method and the building, and must come from the competent professional. Document any ongoing moisture and prevent premature reinstatement of finishes.

instruction.heading: 10. Mould prevention and concealed damage
instruction.body: Musty odour, staining, repeated moisture events and concealed cavities can signal conditions that need specialist investigation. Do not disturb suspect materials in order to prove a hypothesis. File a hidden-damage referral that records the scope exclusions and the route for notifying the occupants. Pause the normal restoration work and escalate any suspected hidden microbial contamination to a competent professional. Occupant communication must be factual and must not state that the building is safe.

instruction.heading: 11. Wastewater, debris and lawful disposal
instruction.body: Flood debris can combine ordinary material with sewage contamination, oils, chemical containers and regulated substances. Local collection and discharge permissions cannot be assumed. Separate the hazardous streams and escalate them, and follow only the locally authorised disposal routes. Complete a draft waste manifest that records the source, the storage controls, the authorised carrier and the regulatory checks that remain unanswered. Do not discharge wastewater or place debris in ordinary collection until the route has been confirmed in writing.

instruction.heading: 12. Verification, documentation and handover limits
instruction.body: Cleaning completion, drying verification, hygienic release and building occupancy clearance are separate claims, and each has a different responsible professional. Create a defensible handover that records the work completed, the evidence, the outstanding defects, the referrals made and the customer's acknowledgement. Report actual observations and refer formal clearance to the qualified authority. Do not present the completion of cleaning as proof that the building is dry, hygienic or safe to occupy.

instruction.heading: Stop-work and referral rules for this module
instruction.body: Stop and refer whenever any of these is true: permission to enter or written safety clearance is missing; the contamination is unknown; a structural hazard, a slip or a confined space has not been cleared; an electrical, gas or solar system is water-exposed or has not been licensed for re-energisation; an exposure has occurred or controls are not in place; the equipment or operators are not suitable; porous material is in question; hidden microbial contamination is suspected; a waste route is not yet known; or a party asks for a dry, hygienic or occupancy statement. A stop-work decision is correct. Record it, and restart only after the competent party has confirmed the scope in writing.

procedure: Stop work. Keep people out of any area that has not been released, and do not enter a structurally or electrically unresolved space.
Confirm in writing the site controller, the permissions, the no-entry zones and the safety reports.
Record the water origin, the contamination indicators, the evidence gaps and the competent reviewer. Do not classify contamination from odour or colour.
Do not energise, isolate, reconnect or test electrical, gas or solar equipment. Refer each hazard to the licensed professional.
Confirm PPE, hygiene facilities and exposure controls. If an exposure may have occurred, follow the employer's incident and medical referral procedure.
Record moisture readings with the instrument, method and baseline. Do not treat a single reading as proof of drying.
Quarantine porous items and refer restoration or disposal decisions to an authorised, competent assessor.
Separate hazardous waste streams and route them only by a locally authorised route confirmed in writing.
Issue a handover that separates cleaning completion, drying verification, hygienic release and occupancy clearance, and refers each claim to its responsible party.

workedExamples.situation: A customer request, an insurer authorisation and a professional safety clearance have all been mentioned, but only the customer's request is on file.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What must be established before the scope is set?
workedExamples.reasoning: Treat the three as separate documents. Only the customer's request exists, so the insurer authorisation and the safety clearance are outstanding. Record the scope sheet, the site controller and the outstanding documents, and do not start work on the request alone.

workedExamples.situation: Floodwater looks clear and smells of nothing unusual, and the owner says it is clean river water.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can the water be treated as safe?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. Appearance and smell cannot prove biological safety. Record the owner's statement as an uncertainty, consider the water source and the time since the intrusion, and refer classification to a competent person.

workedExamples.situation: A ceiling looks sound, but water has undermined the flooring and the stairs look slippery.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Is the visual inspection enough to enter?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. Visual inspection is not structural clearance. Exclude the affected areas, record the evacuation paths and request a qualified structural assessment before any entry.

workedExamples.situation: The power has been switched off at the switchboard, and a worker wants to plug in a dehumidifier.
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop. Apparent isolation is not verified isolation, and water-exposed systems can remain hazardous. Do not energise the system. Refer to the licensed professional for clearance before any connection.

workedExamples.situation: A customer asks for a certificate that the house is dry and safe to live in after the cleaning has finished.
workedExamples.reasoning: Only the completed cleaning and the observed conditions. Drying verification, hygienic release and occupancy clearance are separate claims for different professionals. Record the referrals and do not issue the certificate.

workedExamples.situation: A crew plans to put flood debris, including chemical containers, into ordinary household bins.
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop. The debris contains hazardous streams that cannot be assumed to be collectable as ordinary waste. Separate and escalate them, and use only a route confirmed in writing by the authorised carrier.

commonErrors.error: Starting work on a customer request while the insurer authorisation and safety clearance are missing.
commonErrors.prevention: Treat the three documents as separate, and record which are outstanding before any step.

commonErrors.error: Treating clear, odourless water as biologically safe.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the contamination as uncertain and refer classification to a competent person.

commonErrors.error: Entering a space that looks sound after water has undermined it.
commonErrors.prevention: Visual inspection is not structural clearance. Exclude and request a qualified assessment.

commonErrors.error: Energising a system that appears to be switched off after water exposure.
commonErrors.prevention: Do not energise. Refer to the licensed professional for clearance.

commonErrors.error: Using equipment because it has enough capacity.
commonErrors.prevention: Select equipment by contamination, location, electrical supply and operator training.

commonErrors.error: Relying on a wipe-down to show that porous contents are restored.
commonErrors.prevention: Quarantine porous items and refer the decision to an authorised, competent assessor.

commonErrors.error: Covering a surface before it is dry, which traps moisture.
commonErrors.prevention: Use a monitoring chart and do not reinstate finishes until the trend is confirmed by a competent person.

commonErrors.error: Putting flood debris, including chemical containers, into ordinary bins.
commonErrors.prevention: Separate the hazardous streams and use only a route confirmed in writing.

commonErrors.error: Telling a customer that cleaning completion means the house is dry and safe.
commonErrors.prevention: Separate cleaning completion, drying verification, hygienic release and occupancy clearance, and refer each claim.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: This module does not grant authority to enter, restore, energise, isolate, dispose or certify any flood-affected building or system. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.

Electrical and gas work, structural assessment, sewage handling and some waste disposal are restricted to licensed or specially authorised people. Under the model WHS laws, a PCBU must ensure, so far as reasonably practicable, the health and safety of workers and others. Re-energisation of a water-affected system needs licensed clearance. WorkSafe Victoria's flood page (reviewed 20 January 2023) says not to restore power or gas until a licensed electrician has tested the property wiring and a licensed gasfitter has checked the gas installation; that is Victorian guidance.

The sources include Australian guidance from Comcare, WorkSafe Victoria, the Victorian Building and Plumbing Commission and SafeWork NSW, and UK and US guidance. WorkSafe Victoria's flood page was read directly on 2026-11-03 and supports the Victorian points on switchboards, reconnection, hand washing, PPE, unknown substances and waste, and asbestos removalists. Victorian and NSW sources are state-specific, and the UK and US sources are not Australian law.
No moisture threshold, drying pass value or pathogen clearance value is given in this lesson. Those values come from the competent professional and the applicable standard.
No chemical, dilution, quantity or cleaning formula is given.
A cleaning completion, a drying reading or a visual inspection is not a clearance for hygienic release, structural safety, electrical safety or occupancy.

summary: Scope starts with documented site authority. Customer requests, insurer authorisations and safety clearances are separate.
Water appearance and smell do not prove safety. Contamination stays uncertain until a competent person classifies it.
Visual inspection is not structural clearance. Exclude and refer.
Water-affected electrical and gas systems stay de-energised until licensed clearance is given.
Exposure controls follow the site assessment, training and the facilities that exist.
A moisture reading needs its method. A single number does not prove drying or occupancy.
Select equipment by suitability and training, not by capacity.
Porous items may hold contamination a wipe does not remove.
Drying is a trend, not a finish. Covering too early traps moisture.
Route waste lawfully. Separate hazardous streams.
Report completed work. Refer clearance to qualified authorities.

officialReferences.title: Duties of a person conducting a business or undertaking (PCBU)
officialReferences.covers: Confirms the PCBU duty to workers and others so far as reasonably practicable, and refers to the hierarchy of control. It does not say PPE is a last resort. Check your state or territory WHS regulator for the adopted law. Publisher: Safe Work Australia.

officialReferences.title: Floods and other natural disasters
officialReferences.pageDate: Reviewed on 20/01/2023 (the only date shown; the page was last updated on 20 January 2023)
officialReferences.covers: Read directly on 2026-11-03 (fetched and quoted, not a summary). Covers: do not touch water-damaged switchboards; do not reconnect power or gas until a licensed electrician has tested the wiring and a licensed gasfitter has checked the gas installation; wash hands after contact with flood water or contaminated items; use enclosed footwear, eye protection and gloves; avoid unknown substances and keep them apart from general waste; use a licensed asbestos removalist. Does not cover structural assessment, flood depth or who certifies a building as safe to enter. Victorian guidance only. Publisher: WorkSafe Victoria.

officialReferences.title: Floods and other natural disasters (SafeWork NSW media release on flood clean-up hazards)
officialReferences.covers: Read via summary fetch. SafeWork NSW media release (page metadata shows the same publication and modification date). It lists flood clean-up hazards: contaminated floodwater and sewage, broken glass and debris, damaged electricity and gas or electrical appliances, asbestos (particularly in buildings built before 1990 and in storm-damaged structures), wet or unstable surfaces, wild animals and fatigue. It advises planning before entry, training workers, using licensed asbestos removalists, and not using damaged appliances until an electrician or plumber declares them safe. It does not address structural assessment or who certifies a building as safe to enter.

officialReferences.title: Floods
officialReferences.covers: Read via summary fetch. Comcare page listing flood clean-up hazards (asbestos, flooded sewerage, toxic chemicals, bacteria and pollutants), the PCBU duties to confirm electrical clearance, identify hazardous chemicals and likely asbestos, brief workers on PPE and first aid, and provide clean water and hand hygiene facilities, and the PPE list (rubber-soled shoes, gloves, eye and face protection, respiratory protection and other items). It does not mention mould or give structural assessment points for damaged buildings.

knowledgeChecks.question: A customer request is on file, but the insurer authorisation and the professional safety clearance are not. What should happen first?
options: Start the work, because the customer has asked and the customer is waiting for the crew to arrive on site
Start the drying and sort out the paperwork later, since the drying cannot wait for the approvals
Record the scope sheet and the outstanding documents, and do not start on the customer request alone.

knowledgeChecks.question: Floodwater looks clear and has no odour, and the owner says it is clean river water. What is the correct response?
options: Record the owner's statement as an uncertainty and refer the classification to a competent person.
Treat it as safe, because it looks clean and the water has no smell at all in the room today
Treat it as safe if the owner signs a statement, since the owner knows where the water came from

knowledgeChecks.question: A ceiling looks sound, but water has undermined the flooring. Is a visual inspection enough to enter?
options: Yes, if the ceiling looks sound, since the ceiling is above the floor and is the main concern
No. Visual inspection is not structural clearance. Exclude the area and request a qualified assessment.
Yes, if the worker walks carefully and keeps to the edges of the room where the boards are firm

knowledgeChecks.question: The power has been switched off at the board, and a worker wants to plug in a dehumidifier. What is correct?
options: Plug it in, because the power is off at the board and the dehumidifier needs to start drying the room now
Plug it in at the outlet that is still dry, since that outlet is far from the water on the floor
Stop. Apparent isolation is not verified isolation, and the system is not energised without licensed clearance.

knowledgeChecks.question: A moisture reading shows a low number after drying. What can it establish?
options: Only that a single reading was taken. It needs its method, baseline and interpretation by a competent person.
That the building is dry and safe to occupy, since the reading shows the moisture is now low enough
That the finish can be reinstated now, since the reading is low enough for the job to proceed today

knowledgeChecks.question: A company proposes equipment because it has the largest capacity. What is the right selection test?
options: Choose the largest capacity, because it works fastest and gets the drying finished sooner on site
Choose by contamination, location, electrical supply and operator training, and record the matrix.
Choose the cheapest option available on the day, since the budget is limited for the whole job

knowledgeChecks.question: A wet sofa and insulation are cleaned with a wipe-down. Is the wipe-down enough to show that the items are restored?
options: Yes, because the surface looks clean and the items have been wiped down by the crew this morning
Yes, if the owner agrees to accept the items as they are, since they look fine to them and they want them back
No. Porous items can keep contamination not visible on the surface. Quarantine them and refer the decision.

knowledgeChecks.question: A surface is covered with new lining while it is still damp. What is the risk?
options: Moisture can be trapped and damage concealed. Monitor the trend and do not reinstate until a competent person confirms it.
None, because the lining protects the surface from the air and any further damage that might occur later on
The lining will dry the surface faster, since it holds the heat in and speeds up the whole drying process

knowledgeChecks.question: Musty odour and staining appear behind a wall after a flood. What should be done?
options: Open the wall to see the problem, since the crew needs to know exactly what is happening behind it
Refer the concealed damage for specialist investigation and do not disturb suspect material to prove a hypothesis.
Paint over the staining, since the paint will seal the wall and stop the smell from coming through

knowledgeChecks.question: A crew plans to put flood debris, including chemical containers, into ordinary household bins. What is correct?
options: Do it, because household bins are collected weekly and the crew needs to clear the site today
Do it if the containers are empty, since empty containers can go into ordinary household bins
Stop. Separate the hazardous streams and use only a route confirmed in writing by the authorised carrier.

knowledgeChecks.question: A customer asks for a certificate that the house is dry and safe to live in after the cleaning. What can be written?
options: Only the completed cleaning and observed conditions, with drying, hygienic release and occupancy clearance referred to their responsible parties.
A certificate that the house is dry and safe to live in, since the cleaning was done properly and the team checked every room in the house
A certificate for the cleaned rooms that the owner can show to the insurer, so the claim can be closed quickly and the cleaning is accepted

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker has a possible exposure during water removal. What must happen?
options: Finish the task and report at the end of the shift, since the crew is almost done and the exposure seems minor
Stop the exposure work, follow the employer's incident and medical referral procedure, and keep the record confidential.
Wash the skin and continue without a record, since the water was clean and the exposure was very short and the worker felt fine after the work
